turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?
turns.patient_response:
Hey, yeah, thanks for seeing me. Um, so I guess I came in because I just feel like I’m literally crawling out of my skin whenever I’m supposed to sit still. Like, especially when I'm in the radiology suite or in my classes. Actually, the chairs in my anatomy lecture are the absolute worst. They have those tiny little desks attached to them, you know? The ones that barely fit a notebook, let alone a laptop, and my laptop is this huge gaming rig because I like to play Valorant between my clinical shifts—I'm actually trying to rank up to Ascendant right now, it's been a massive grind and my team keeps throwing. 

But anyway, what was I... right, sitting still. Yeah, after months of just trying to tough it out and just stay in my seat like everyone else, I still end up pacing around the control room, or shifting constantly, or just finding literally any random excuse to get up and move. I just can't stay put.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient states they find 'any random excuse to get up and move' and 'just can't stay put' in situations where they are expected to remain seated, like classes or the radiology suite.

turns.doctor_question: How far back does this feeling of not being able to sit still go? Has it been something you've dealt with since you were a kid, or is this more of a recent thing that started in college or medical school?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, it goes way, way back. Like, my parents still talk about my elementary school parent-teacher conferences. The teachers were always telling them I was constantly out of my seat, calling out answers, or just rushing ahead on worksheets before they even finished giving the directions. So it was happening way before middle school, definitely not just something that started with my radiology training. 

Actually, speaking of elementary school, do you remember those giant rainbow parachutes we used to play with in gym class? Man, those were the absolute best. We’d all lift it up and run underneath, and it felt like being inside a weird colorful tent. Gym was the only class I actually liked because we could just go crazy, though I got in trouble once for climbing the folded-up bleachers. They look exactly like giant stairs, how are you *not* supposed to climb them, right? I think the gym teacher blew his whistle right in my ear that time. My ears were ringing for like an hour. 

But yeah... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, how long it's been happening. Yeah, definitely since I was a little kid.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets distracted by unrelated thoughts about gym class and forgets the doctor's question.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient recalls teachers saying they were 'constantly out of my seat' during elementary school.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes inappropriately climbing the folded-up bleachers in gym class.

turns.doctor_question: Beyond just the physical restlessness you've described, has this difficulty sitting still actually caused problems for you—like affecting your grades, your relationships, or your ability to complete tasks that require focus?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, it's actually getting really bad. Like, my clinical evaluations have taken a massive hit lately. They even put me on this formal remediation plan, which sounds like something out of a sci-fi movie, right? Like "commence remediation." I was watching *Dune* the other night, have you seen it? The sound design in that movie is absolutely insane, it literally vibrates your chest when you watch it in IMAX. I spent like three hours watching behind-the-scenes videos on how they made the sand worm sounds. They used, like, a microphone buried in actual sand or something crazy like that. I really want to upgrade my gaming headset to get that kind of bass for Valorant. 

But wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the clinic stuff. Yeah, the remediation plan. My supervisors are saying my behavior disrupts the patient flow and makes teamwork way harder. Because I'm always pacing around or just... not standing exactly where I'm supposed to be when they need me to prep the room. Like last week, we had this portable chest X-ray up in the ICU, and those portable machines are basically like driving a giant electric shopping cart. They are so heavy, and the front wheels always squeak. I actually tried spraying WD-40 on one once because the noise was driving me crazy, but the hospital maintenance guy got super mad at me. 

Anyway... yeah, I’m just really worried it could cost me my place in the program if I don’t get it under control. So it's definitely causing some real problems right now.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts, going on long tangents about a movie and an X-ray machine before losing their train of thought.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient admits to 'not standing exactly where I'm supposed to be' when expected to remain in place to prep a room.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly states that they are 'always pacing around' at work.

turns.doctor_question: When you're trying to focus on something—like reading a textbook chapter or watching a lecture—do you find it hard to keep your attention on it, or do you find yourself getting distracted easily, even when you're not feeling restless?
turns.patient_response:
Um, reading a textbook? No, honestly, I don't really have a problem with that. Like, if I'm reading something, I can usually just read it. It's more about the physical part, you know? Just sitting there. Like, my eyes work fine, my brain reads the words, but my body is just... vibrating. 

Speaking of vibrating, did you know that cats purr at a frequency that actually promotes bone healing? I read that somewhere on Reddit. It's like 25 to 140 Hertz or something. I was thinking about that the other day in the clinic when we were doing a bone scan on this guy's tibia. Like, imagine if instead of casts, they just strapped a bunch of purring cats to your leg. That would be insane. My roommate has a cat, actually. Her name is Sir Meows-a-Lot, which is hilarious because it's a girl cat, but whatever. She always tries to sit on my keyboard when I'm playing Valorant, right when I'm trying to hold an angle with an Operator. It's so annoying, but she's really soft. 

But yeah, anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, focusing. Yeah, no, I don't really get distracted like that, it's just the sitting still part that kills me.

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes feeling a physical restlessness, stating their body is 'vibrating' and that 'sitting still... kills me'.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, going on a long, unprompted tangent about cats, bone healing, and video games before returning to the question.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly denies having trouble sustaining attention, stating they can 'usually just read' a textbook without a problem.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly denies being easily distracted, stating 'I don't really get distracted like that'.

turns.doctor_question: Beyond the restlessness and difficulty sitting still, do you find yourself acting without thinking first? Like interrupting people, making impulsive decisions, or doing risky things without considering the consequences?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, oh my gosh, all the time. It's actually a huge problem in the clinic right now. Like, when my supervisor is explaining a positioning step for a scan, or if they start asking me a question about the protocol, I'll just jump right in and blurt out the answer before they're even done talking. And then, of course, I realize I completely missed the second half of their sentence, which is usually the part that actually mattered. 

It's like my mouth is moving faster than my brain, you know? Sort of like when you're playing a first-person shooter and you just start spraying bullets before you even have your crosshairs on the guy. I play a lot of Valorant, I think I mentioned that. I main Jett, mostly because her movement abilities are so fast. You can literally just dash into a site and cause absolute chaos. My friend Dave always yells at me because I'll dash in without waiting for him to throw his flashbang first, and then I just get instantly headshot. Dave's actually thinking about dropping out of his engineering program to start a Twitch channel, which I think is a terrible idea, but he bought this ridiculous $400 microphone for it. It has this crazy RGB lighting that syncs up with his gameplay. 

Wait, what was the question? Something about acting without thinking? Yeah, so, the blurting things out before my supervisors finish talking. That definitely happens a lot. I just can't seem to wait my turn to speak.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets distracted by unrelated thoughts about a video game and their friend, completely losing track of the doctor's original question.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states they jump in and blurt out answers before their supervisor is done talking.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient admits, 'I just can't seem to wait my turn to speak.'
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient describes interrupting their supervisor by jumping right in while they are still explaining or asking a question.

turns.doctor_question: When you're working on a task that requires sustained attention—like studying for an exam or reading through a patient's imaging report—do you find yourself losing track of what you're doing, forgetting what you just read, or having trouble organizing your thoughts? Or is it really just the physical restlessness that's the main issue?
turns.patient_response:
Honestly, no. Reading the reports or studying is fine. I don't forget what I just read or anything like that, and my thoughts are pretty organized. It's really just the physical stuff. Like, if I'm reading a report, my brain is totally focused on the words, but my knee is just bouncing a million miles an hour under the desk. 

I actually wore a hole straight through the bottom of my favorite pair of sneakers just from rubbing my foot against the metal leg of the desk in the radiology reading room. They were these limited edition Nike Dunks, too. The Panda ones. I was so mad. The resale value on those is crazy right now, like way more than I can afford on a student budget. I tried to use this special shoe glue to fix the sole, but it looked terrible and smelled like super strong chemicals. It actually gave my roommate Dave a massive headache, so I had to leave them out on our balcony to air out, and then it randomly downpoured that night. They got completely soaked. So that was a total disaster. I just ended up throwing them away. 

But anyway... wait, did I answer your question? Yeah, no, I don't really lose track of what I'm doing when I have to read or study. My focus is fine, it's just my body that won't chill out.

turns.patient_response:
No, getting started and organizing stuff isn't really an issue for me. I actually like planning things out, it's pretty natural. Like, I have this whole color-coded system for my clinic schedule and my classes. It works great. I use Google Calendar, mostly because you can sync it with everything. 

Speaking of Google, did you know they started out in a garage? Like, literally just a rented garage in California. It's crazy to think about. I was watching this documentary about Silicon Valley the other day, and it's wild how many huge tech companies started that way. Apple, Amazon, HP. It makes me feel like I should be doing something more productive with my garage back home. Right now, it's just full of my dad's old woodworking tools that he never uses. He bought this massive table saw like five years ago because he was going to build custom birdhouses, but he made exactly one birdhouse and then gave up because a squirrel moved into it instead of a bird. The squirrel was actually super aggressive, it would throw acorns at our dog. Our dog is a golden retriever, so he's basically completely harmless, he just wanted to be friends with it. 

But yeah, wait, what were you asking? Oh, planning and organizing. Yeah, no, I'm good at that. I don't forget what I'm supposed to do or have trouble starting things. It's just the sitting still part that's the problem.
